title: Midae aures
titleEn: The Ears of Midas — Metamorphoses XI.146–193
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Midas, having come to hate riches, has taken himself off to the woods and to Pan, and his wits are as thick as they ever were. Pan boasts his pipes above Apollo's lyre, the mountain-god Tmolus sits as judge and gives the verdict to the lyre, and Midas alone speaks against it — for which Apollo draws his ears out long, fills them with whitening hair and gives them the power to move. He tries to hide them under purple turbans, but the slave who trims his hair has seen, and, unable to tell and unable to keep quiet, whispers the secret into a hole in the ground. A grove of reeds grows over the spot, and when the year is full the south wind makes them repeat the buried words.

sentences.t:
Ille, perosus opes, silvas et rura colebat
Panaque montanis habitantem semper in antris.
sentences.l: He, having come to hate riches, haunted the woods and the fields, and worshipped Pan, dwelling always in mountain caves.
sentences.i: Sick of riches, he took to the woods and the open country, and to Pan, who is always at home in his mountain caves.
sentences.n: One verb, colebat, governs both objects but in two different senses: to frequent or live in (the woods and fields) and to worship (Pan). English has no single verb that carries both, so the literal supplies two. perosus is the participle of perodi and is active in sense, “having come to hate”, not “hated by”. Pana is the Greek form of the accusative of the name, as Midan is at 162.

sentences.t:
Pingue sed ingenium mansit, nocituraque, ut ante,
rursus erant domino stultae praecordia mentis.
sentences.l: But the dull nature stayed, and, as before, the vitals of his foolish mind were once again going to do their owner harm.
sentences.i: But the thick wits remained: as before, the inward parts of that foolish mind were set to hurt their owner all over again.
sentences.n: nocitura is the future participle of nocere, agreeing with the neuter plural praecordia; with erant it makes the periphrastic “were going to harm”. nocere takes the dative, which is why the owner appears as domino. praecordia, literally the parts lying in front of the heart, is plural in form for a single seat of feeling; pingue is literally “fat”, used here of a mind that is slow.

sentences.t:
Nam freta prospiciens late riget arduus alto
Tmolus in adscensu, clivoque extensus utroque
Sardibus hinc, illinc parvis finitur Hypaepis.
sentences.l: For, looking out far over the straits, Tmolus stands stiff and steep in high ascent, and, stretched out on either slope, is bounded on this side by Sardis, on that by little Hypaepa.
sentences.i: For Tmolus rises rigid and sheer along its climb, gazing far out over the sea, and, spreading down both its slopes, ends at Sardis on one side and at little Hypaepa on the other.
sentences.n: alto stands as the last word of 150 and the noun it belongs to, adscensu, in the line below — the phrase steps over the line-end, which is how the sentence keeps moving. riget is literally “is stiff”, used of the mountain standing rigid; arduus is a nominative adjective describing Tmolus where English would rather have an adverb, “steeply”. finitur is passive and takes the ablatives Sardibus and Hypaepis, “is bounded by”.

sentences.t:
Pan ibi dum teneris iactat sua carmina nymphis
et leve cerata modulatur harundine carmen,
ausus Apollineos prae se contemnere cantus,
iudice sub Tmolo certamen venit ad impar.
sentences.l: There, while Pan flings his songs at tender nymphs and plays a light tune on the waxed reed, having dared to despise Apollo's singing in comparison with his own, he comes to an unequal contest, with Tmolus as judge.
sentences.i: There, while Pan is showing off his songs to the young nymphs and piping a light air on his waxed reed, he goes so far as to rate Apollo's music below his own — and so comes to an unequal contest, with Tmolus for judge.
sentences.n: iactat is “throws about”, the ordinary word for vaunting, with the dative teneris nymphis for the audience he throws them at. cerata harundine is the ablative of the instrument, the reed pipes joined with wax. prae se is literally “in front of himself”, that is, “in comparison with his own”. ausus is the participle of audeo, a semi-deponent: passive in form, active in sense, “having dared”. In the last line the adjective impar is held back to the very end, with the verb and the preposition ad standing between it and its noun certamen, so that the word “unequal” lands last. Magnus prints carmina at 153, “songs”; some editions print sibila, “whistlings, hissings”, which makes Pan's own music sound thinner than he thinks it is.

sentences.t:
Monte suo senior iudex consedit et aures
liberat arboribus:
sentences.l: On his own mountain the elder sat down as judge and frees his ears from the trees:
sentences.i: The old god took his seat as judge on his own mountain and clears the trees away from his ears:
sentences.n: senior, the comparative of senex, stands as a noun beside iudex: “the elder, as judge”. consedit is perfect and liberat present in the same sentence — the slipping between past narrative and vivid present runs all through this part, and it is not a mistake. arboribus is an ablative of separation with liberat. The judge is the mountain itself, so the trees he clears from his ears are his own woods, as the next lines and 164 confirm.

sentences.t:
quercu coma caerula tantum
cingitur, et pendent circum cava tempora glandes.
sentences.l: with oak alone is his dark-blue hair encircled, and acorns hang around his hollow temples.
sentences.i: Oak alone binds his dark green hair, and acorns dangle about his hollow temples.
sentences.n: caerulus is properly the dark blue of sea and sky; here it colours the mountain's leafy hair, so English wants something like “dark green”. tantum, “only”, limits the wreath to oak and nothing else. cingitur is passive, “is encircled”, with coma caerula for its subject; glandes, the subject of pendent, is held to the very end of the line, after both the verb and the phrase circum cava tempora.

sentences.t:
Isque deum pecoris spectans “in indice” dixit
“nulla mora est.”
sentences.l: And he, gazing at the god of the flock, said, “in the one who declares there is no delay.”
sentences.i: And, with his eyes on the god of the flock, he said, “The one who is to declare will not hold things up.”
sentences.n: deum here is the accusative singular of deus, the object of spectans, not the genitive plural “of the gods”; pecoris is the genitive with it, and the god of the flock is Pan. Magnus prints in indice, “in the one who points out or declares”; some editions print in iudice, “in the judge”, naming Tmolus by the office he has just taken. Either way the sense is that the judge is ready and nothing holds the contest up. The same root comes back as indicium, “the thing that gives it away”, at 188.

sentences.t:
Calamis agrestibus insonat ille
barbaricoque Midan (aderat nam forte canenti)
carmine delenit.
sentences.l: He makes his rustic reeds sound out, and with barbarous song charms Midas (for he happened to be present as he sang).
sentences.i: He sets his country reeds sounding, and with that outlandish tune he wins Midas over — Midas happened to be there to hear him sing.
sentences.n: insonat is intransitive, “makes a noise”, and calamis agrestibus is the ablative of what he makes it on. The adjective barbarico opens 162 and the noun it belongs to, carmine, opens 163, with the object Midan and the whole parenthesis standing between them. barbaricus means simply “foreign, not Greek”, and it is not neutral here: it sets Phrygian piping against Apollo's lyre before the contest is decided. aderat governs the dative canenti, “was present to him as he sang”. Midan is the Greek form of the accusative of the name, which Ovid keeps.

sentences.t:
Post hunc sacer ora retorsit
Tmolus ad os Phoebi:
sentences.l: After him holy Tmolus twisted his face round toward the mouth of Phoebus:
sentences.i: After him holy Tmolus turned his face round to Phoebus' lips:
sentences.n: ora is the plural of os used of a single face, and the same word returns in the singular a little later in the same sentence, os Phoebi — the mountain's face turning toward the god's mouth. retorsit is “twisted back”, a heavier verb than English “turned”, and it is doing work: the thing being turned is a mountainside.

sentences.t: vultum sua silva secuta est.
sentences.l: his own forest followed his countenance.
sentences.i: his woods turned with his face.
sentences.n: sua silva, “his own wood”, is the subject; secuta est is the perfect of the deponent sequor, passive in form but active in meaning, “followed”. This is the line that makes the earlier picture literal: the god's face is a mountainside and the trees swing round with it.

sentences.t:
Ille caput flavum lauro Parnaside vinctus
verrit humum Tyrio saturata murice palla,
instrictamque fidem gemmis et dentibus Indis
sustinet a laeva;
sentences.l: He, bound as to his golden head with Parnassian laurel, sweeps the ground with a robe steeped in Tyrian purple, and holds up from the left the lyre bound in with gems and Indian teeth;
sentences.i: He, his golden head wreathed in laurel from Parnassus, sweeps the ground with a robe soaked in Tyrian purple, and in his left hand holds up the lyre set with gems and Indian ivory;
sentences.n: caput flavum is an accusative of respect with the passive participle vinctus — literally “bound as to his head”, that is, “with his head bound”. It is a Greek turn that Latin verse borrows when a passive participle needs to name the part affected. murex is the shellfish that yields the purple, so saturata murice is “soaked with the dye”. dentibus Indis, “Indian teeth”, is ivory. a laeva is “from the left side”. Magnus prints instrictam, from instringere, roughly “bound on”; some editions print instructam, “fitted out, inlaid”.

sentences.t: tenuit manus altera plectrum.
sentences.l: the other hand held the plectrum.
sentences.n: altera is “the other of the two”, so the phrase means the right hand without naming it. tenuit is perfect where verrit and sustinet just before it are present — the same slipping between tenses as at 157 and 158.

sentences.t: Artificis status ipse fuit.
sentences.l: His very stance was an artist's.
sentences.i: His bearing by itself was that of an artist.
sentences.n: artificis is a bare genitive standing as the predicate after fuit: literally “the stance itself was of an artist”, where English says “an artist's” or “that of an artist”. Latin uses the genitive this way to say what a thing is characteristic of, and the same turn returns at 178, cetera sunt hominis. ipse strengthens status — the pose alone, before a note has been played, since the plucking of the strings only begins in the next clause.

sentences.t:
Tum stamina docto
pollice sollicitat, quorum dulcedine captus
Pana iubet Tmolus citharae submittere cannas.
sentences.l: Then he stirs the strings with skilled thumb, and Tmolus, caught by their sweetness, orders Pan to lower his reeds to the lyre.
sentences.i: Then with a practised thumb he sets the strings going, and Tmolus, caught by their sweetness, tells Pan to bow his pipes to the lyre.
sentences.n: stamina are properly the upright threads of a loom, used here of the lyre's strings; sollicitat is “keeps working at, stirs”. quorum is a linking relative reaching back to stamina and is the genitive with dulcedine, “by the sweetness of which”, where English wants “and, caught by their sweetness”; dulcedine is the ablative of cause with captus, which agrees with Tmolus. submittere with the dative citharae is “to put lower than, to make yield to”, so the verdict comes out as an order that Pan's reeds give way to the lyre.

sentences.l: The judgement and the verdict of the holy mountain pleases everyone, yet it is arraigned and called unjust by the talk of one man, Midas;
sentences.i: Everyone is satisfied with the decision and the holy mountain's verdict; but one man's talk — Midas's — attacks it and calls it unfair;
sentences.n: placet is singular although two subjects, iudicium and sententia, stand with it, one on either side of the verb: Latin will often let the verb agree with a single one of two subjects. The two passives that follow, arguitur and vocatur, have sententia alone for their subject, as the feminine iniusta shows. unius opens 174 and its noun Midae comes two words later, so the whole weight of the line falls on the single dissenting voice.

sentences.t:
nec Delius aures
humanam stolidas patitur retinere figuram,
sed trahit in spatium villisque albentibus implet
instabilesque imas facit et dat posse moveri,
cetera sunt hominis:
sentences.l: Nor does the Delian suffer the dull ears to keep a human shape, but draws them out into length, and fills them with whitening hair, and makes them unsteady at their lowest part, and gives them the power to be moved; the rest is a man's:
sentences.i: The Delian will not let those stupid ears keep a human shape: he pulls them out long, fills them with whitish hair, makes them loose at the root and gives them the power to move. The rest of him is a man's:
sentences.n: Delius is Apollo, named from Delos. aures at the end of 174 and its adjective stolidas in 175 are split across the line-end, with humanam standing between them and its own noun figuram closing the line — the two pairs are interlocked. stolidas, “dull, stupid”, is attached to the ears though it describes their owner. patitur is deponent, active in meaning, “allows”. imas, “lowest”, belongs to the ears and means their base, where they join the head. dat posse moveri is a compressed idiom, literally “gives to be able to be moved”, the infinitive standing as the object of dat. cetera sunt hominis is the predicate genitive again, as at 169: “the rest is a man's”.

sentences.t:
partem damnatur in unam
induiturque aures lente gradientis aselli.
sentences.l: in one part he is condemned, and he is clothed in the ears of a slowly-stepping little ass.
sentences.i: his sentence falls on one part: he is fitted with the ears of a slow-plodding ass.
sentences.n: partem and its adjective unam are split by the preposition in, which stands between them along with the verb — a common verse order, and here it lets “one part” frame the whole clause. induitur is passive in form but takes the accusative aures: the so-called middle use, where the subject has the thing put on him or puts it on himself. aselli is the diminutive of asinus, “little ass”, and the diminutive is contemptuous and comic, not affectionate; lente gradientis, “slowly stepping”, is the genitive participle describing the animal.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem celare cupit, turpisque pudore
tempora purpureis temptat velare tiaris.
sentences.l: He indeed longs to hide it, and, made ugly, out of shame he tries to veil his temples with purple turbans.
sentences.i: He wants to hide it, of course — ugly now, and ashamed, he tries to cover his temples with purple turbans.
sentences.n: turpis is nominative and describes Midas himself as disfigured, while pudore is a separate ablative of cause, “out of shame”. Magnus prints turpisque; some editions print turpique, which would attach the adjective to pudore instead and give “out of shameful embarrassment”, moving the ugliness from the man to his feeling. The tiara is an eastern headdress with side-flaps that can be brought down over the ears, which is the point of it here. Where Magnus has velare, “to veil”, some editions have relevare, “to lighten, relieve”.

sentences.t:
Sed solitus longos ferro resecare capillos
viderat hoc famulus.
sentences.l: But the servant accustomed to cut his long hair with iron had seen this.
sentences.i: But the slave whose work was trimming his long hair with the blade had seen it.
sentences.n: solitus is the participle of soleo, a semi-deponent like ausus at 155: passive in form, active in sense, “having been accustomed”. ferro, “with iron”, names the metal for the tool, the shears or blade. The subject famulus is held back to the last word of its sentence, so the man is defined entirely by his job before we are told he is a servant at all.

sentences.t:
Qui cum nec prodere visum
dedecus auderet, cupiens efferre sub auras,
nec posset reticere tamen, secedit humumque
effodit et, domini quales adspexerit aures,
voce refert parva terraeque inmurmurat haustae,
sentences.l: And he, since he neither dared to betray the disgrace he had seen — longing though he was to bring it out under the open air — nor yet could keep silent, goes apart and digs up the ground, and what sort of ears he had looked upon on his master he tells in a small voice and murmurs to the scooped-out earth,
sentences.i: He did not dare give away the shameful thing he had seen, though he was longing to bring it out into the open, and he could not keep it in either; so he goes off alone, digs up the ground and, in a low voice, tells what sort of ears he has seen on his master, murmuring it down into the earth he has scooped out.
sentences.n: Qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and he”, not “who”. The cum-clause takes the subjunctive (auderet, posset) and gives the reason: neither daring to speak nor able to stay quiet. The participle visum agrees with dedecus and is split from it across the line-end, 183 to 184. quales with the perfect subjunctive adspexerit is an indirect question depending on refert, “he reports what sort of ears he had seen”. terrae is the dative after inmurmurat, “murmurs into the earth”, and haustae agrees with it, from haurire, “to draw out”, of the earth he has scooped from the hole. voce and its adjective parva are split around the verb refert, so the small voice is itself broken apart in the line.

sentences.t:
indiciumque suae vocis tellure regesta
obruit et scrobibus tacitus discedit opertis.
sentences.l: and buries the evidence of his own voice with the earth thrown back, and goes silently away with the trench covered over.
sentences.i: Then he heaps the soil back over the evidence of his own voice and walks away in silence with the trench filled in.
sentences.n: tellure regesta and scrobibus opertis are both ablative absolutes — self-contained “with X done” phrases where English wants a clause. indicium is “the thing that points it out, the give-away”, from the same root as the indice of 160. tacitus is a nominative adjective describing the man where English wants an adverb, “in silence”; obruit here is the verb the reeds will undo at 193.

sentences.t:
Creber harundinibus tremulis ibi surgere lucus
coepit et, ut primum pleno maturuit anno,
prodidit agricolam:
sentences.l: A grove thick with quivering reeds began to rise there, and, as soon as it ripened with the year full, it betrayed the farmer:
sentences.i: A grove thick with trembling reeds began to spring up there, and the moment it came ripe with the full year, it gave the farmer away:
sentences.n: creber takes the ablative harundinibus for what it is crowded with, “thick with reeds”. ut primum is “as soon as”, and pleno anno an ablative of time, “when the year was complete”. agricola properly means a tiller of the soil, and it is a wry choice: the only ground-work this servant did was the digging and refilling of the hole in 186 and 189.

sentences.t:
leni nam motus ab austro
obruta verba refert dominique coarguit aures.
sentences.l: for, moved by the gentle south wind, it reports the buried words and convicts its master's ears.
sentences.i: for, stirred by a soft south wind, it repeats the buried words and convicts its master's ears.
sentences.n: nam stands second in its clause rather than first, and leni is separated from its noun austro by three words — ordinary verse freedom. motus is the perfect participle of movere agreeing with the grove. The verb refert is the one used of the servant at 187, and obruta picks up his own obruit at 189: the reeds do exactly what he did, and undo it. coarguit is stronger than “report” — it is to prove a thing beyond denial, the word for convicting someone, and both layers keep it.
